title: Buoyancy removes the physical barrier to size in fully aquatic animals

fields.label: Label
fields.value: Buoyancy removes the physical barrier to size in fully aquatic animals

fields.label: Statement
fields.value: An animal wholly immersed in water whose density about matches the water, like a whale, has its weight counterpoised, so there is no longer a physical barrier to its indefinite growth in size.

fields.label: Quotation
fields.value: Under these circumstances there is no longer a physical barrier to the indefinite growth in magnitude of the animal.

fields.label: Agent
fields.value: delphisci On Growth and Form claim extractor

fields.label: Assumptions
fields.value: D’Arcy Wentworth Thompson, On Growth and Form (1st ed., Cambridge: Cambridge University Press, 1917), Chapter II, “On Magnitude”; topic “Strength, weight and size limits”. Scope: fully aquatic animals of near-neutral buoyancy, e.g. whales

fields.label: Assessment
fields.value: GPT-5.6 Sol on thompson1917-ch02-04: partially-resolvable, resolvability 0.51

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: Public trait data and mechanics can establish that buoyancy relaxes weight support, but cannot confirm absence of every physical barrier. The strongest empirical test addresses a restricted interpretation rather than literal indefinite growth.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Compare maximum body size and structural safety factors across neutrally buoyant aquatic and terrestrial taxa, and model how buoyancy changes skeletal loading. Evidence that another physical constraint imposes a finite aquatic size bound would refute indefinite physical growth, while reduced gravity loading alone supports only the narrower premise.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Hydrodynamic, feeding, oxygen and tissue constraints remain despite buoyancy.

Indefinite growth is an unobservable limiting assertion.

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: Body masses of whales and land mammals, and some of their skeletons, are public, so the comparative prediction can be examined. The word indefinite has no finite confirming observation: existing size catalogs can show that aquatic maxima exceed terrestrial ones, which they do, without showing that no physical barrier remains. Buoyancy itself is assumed from habit rather than measured, so the test is a proxy for part of the claim.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Compare maximum mass and limb reinforcement of fully aquatic, near-neutrally buoyant mammals with terrestrial mammals. Loss of the gravitational barrier predicts much larger aquatic maxima without the same disproportionate limb bones; a hard aquatic ceiling at terrestrial masses, with the same skeletal scaling, would count against that comparative prediction.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
A large but finite whale is compatible both with no physical barrier and with a high barrier of another kind.

Neutral buoyancy is not measured; life-habit codes are only a coarse proxy.
